newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus in oil crisis, currency rules blamed.
newsitem.headline: Belarus in oil crisis, currency rules blamed.

text.p: Belarus, a former Soviet republic largely dependent on Russia for its supplies, is in deep crisis as its two oil refineries run out of oil mainly due to a currency crunch, industry sources said on Tuesday.

"The two plants are refining 17,000 tonnes of oil a day compared with 35,000-40,000 tonnes between January and October this year," Vladimir Livensky, a vice president of the state oil concern Belnefneprodukt, said. "Reserves will run out in four or five days."
Energy experts blamed the crisis on a host of reasons, including difficulties in converting the country's currency into dollars .
"Russian companies have reduced oil supplies because they have problems converting Belarussian roubles at the currency exchange. Their demands were not met," Livensky said.

The central bank, following a decree by President Alexander Lukashenko, has set an official rate of 13,100 to 15,500 Belarussian roubles to the dollar at a time when the currency fetches 22,500-23,000 in neighbouring Russia and Ukraine.

Another Belnefteprodukt vice president, Vladimir Prokopchuk, told Reuters on Monday he hoped oil supplies would resume because the central bank had converted $22 million of his company's profits into dollars atthe request by Russian oil exporters.
"We hope oil supplies will increase after the conversion, but no earlier than in a week," Livensky said.
"But we cannot expect rivers of Russian oil to flow to Belarus if there are problems with oil even inside Russia."

Russian Deputy Fuel and Energy Minister Valery Garipov said on Tuesday that crude oil exports would fall in December because of a government programme to channel more oil to domestic refineries. He did not say by how much.

The former Soviet republics are often the first to suffer when Russia lower oil exports and the announcement did not augur well for Belarus, which also suffered last month when Russia cut gas supplies by half.
Russia last week resumed regular gas deliveries to its western neighbour Belarus, but only after Minsk paid $10 million of its $50 million gas debt.

Energy experts also blamed the oil crisis on the fact that Russian producers get $102 a tonne for oil sold to Belarus under a special customs agreement when they can obtain about $160 for every tonne sold elsewhere in Europe.
The two refineries in Belarus can handle about 26 million tonnes of oil a year, most of it from Russia, but they are working far below capacity.
The country of 10 million people has also fixed oil prices below world market levels and energy experts say a monopolistic structure in Belarus had contributed to supply crisis.
Lukashenko signed a decree last year authorising only six out of 60 domestic and Russian suppliers to sell oil to Belarus.
"Now there are only six oil exporters left. Supplies are heavily controlled by Russian companies -- Slavneft, LUKoil LKOH.RTS and Yukos," one expert told Reuters.
Belarus, with 1.39 million tonnes of domestic oil output, imports 10 million tonnes of Russian oil a year for its own needs while it refines six million tonnes for Russia.
Belarus oil output this year is forecast at 1.86 million tonnes compared with 1.93 million tonnes in 1995.
